title: EPPS 6356 Assignment 2: Base R Graphics
text:
1. Working through Murrell’s chapter 1 code
The opening examples helped me understand the difference between starting a plot and adding to one. A high-level call such as plot() normally creates a new plot, establishes coordinates, and draws the data, axes, frame, and labels. The scatterplot panel in the standard-plot examples separates these steps: plot.new() opens a blank plot, plot.window() establishes the coordinate ranges, and low-level calls supply the lines, points, axes, frame, and text. This makes the work that a single plot() call normally handles much easier to see.
par() changes the graphics settings rather than drawing observations. For example, mfrow determines how subsequent plots share the device, mar reserves space around each plot, and las controls the orientation of axis labels. These changes become visible when the relevant elements are drawn. Saving the previous settings and restoring them afterward matters because otherwise a later plot may inherit margins, colors, or a layout intended for an earlier example.
The order of commands is especially important in base graphics. My notes initially described the text as simply not appearing when text() came before plot(), but the more precise explanation depends on the device state: without an existing plot, text() produces an error; with one, it adds text to that plot, which a subsequent high-level call can replace. Base graphics draws onto the current device as commands execute, so changing an earlier element usually means drawing the plot again. In ggplot2, layers and settings are normally assembled into a plot object before that object is printed.
Two examples corrected my initial interpretation of the code. In the histogram, freq = FALSE puts the bars on a probability-density scale so that the dnorm() curve uses the same units; a density curve over a count histogram would usually appear compressed near the baseline. Also, boxplot() normally starts a new plot, but boxplot(add = TRUE) adds boxes to the existing coordinates. The function’s behavior therefore depends on its arguments, and the two offset sets of boxes can appear side by side without erasing each other.
The bar-chart example showed that a plotting function can also return useful information. barplot() returns the bar midpoints, which the later mtext() and text() calls use to align labels with the bars. This also clarified the difference between text positioned in the margins and text placed at data coordinates inside the plot. For the surface example, theta changes the horizontal viewing direction, phi changes the viewing elevation, and expand controls the relative height of the surface.
My recorded work covers the introduction and standard base-graphics examples. The notes do not document completed runs of the later lattice, ggplot2, or other package-dependent sections, so I do not report those sections as completed. Those examples require additional plotting systems, packages, or image resources; the discussion here is limited to what the base-graphics notes support.

title: EPPS 6356 Assignment 2: Base R Graphics
text:
2. The plotting functions
Each function below is used on the 2024 Happy Planet Index data. The code that produced every figure is shown with it. The final five examples build up the same GDP–life satisfaction comparison, redrawing the plot in each chunk so that every figure is reproducible.

2.1 Setting up the canvas

par()

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4, 1, 1), las = 1)
hist(hpi$life_exp, breaks = 12, col = "grey80", main = "",
     xlab = "Life expectancy (years), 2024")
hist(hpi$hpi, breaks = 12, col = "lightblue", main = "",
     xlab = "Happy Planet Index, 2024")
par(op)







Figure 1: par() draws nothing itself: it sets the layout, margins, and axis-label orientation that later calls use, which only becomes visible once the two histograms are drawn into the 1 x 2 layout.







box()

plot(hpi$life_exp, hpi$hpi, bty = "n", pch = 16,
     col = "steelblue", xlab = "Life expectancy (years), 2024",
     ylab = "Happy Planet Index, 2024")
box(bty = "l", col = "grey30", lwd = 2)







Figure 2: box() adds a frame to an existing plot; bty = ‘l’ draws only its left and bottom edges.







axis()

plot(hpi$life_exp, hpi$hpi, axes = FALSE, pch = 16,
     col = "steelblue", xlab = "Life expectancy (years), 2024",
     ylab = "Happy Planet Index, 2024")
axis(1, at = seq(50, 90, 10), labels = paste(seq(50, 90, 10), "yr"))
axis(2, at = seq(0, 80, 20), las = 1)
box(bty = "l")







Figure 3: axis() adds axes to an existing plot and controls their sides, tick positions, labels, and label orientation.








2.2 Drawing whole plots

hist()

hist(hpi$life_exp, breaks = 12, col = "grey80", main = "",
     xlab = "Life expectancy (years), 2024")







Figure 4: hist() starts a new plot and groups life expectancy into bins whose bar heights show the number of countries in each interval.







boxplot()

op <- par(mar = c(4.5, 13, 1, 1))
boxplot(hpi ~ continent, data = hpi, horizontal = TRUE,
        las = 1, col = "lightblue", main = "", ylab = "",
        xlab = "Happy Planet Index, 2024", cex.axis = 0.8)
par(op)







Figure 5: boxplot() compares regional HPI distributions through medians, quartiles, whiskers extending to observations within 1.5 interquartile ranges, and points beyond the whiskers.







pie()

region_counts <- table(hpi$continent)
region_labels <- paste0(names(region_counts), " (", region_counts, ")")
pie(region_counts, labels = region_labels,
    col = hcl.colors(length(region_counts), "Pastel 1"),
    radius = 0.65, cex = 0.7, main = "Countries by region, 2024")







Figure 6: pie() shows each region’s share of the 153 country records as a slice, although a bar chart would make comparisons easier because lengths are easier to compare than angles or areas.







persp()

surface_data <- hpi[complete.cases(hpi[c("hpi", "life_exp", "footprint")]), ]
surface_model <- lm(hpi ~ life_exp + footprint, data = surface_data)
xs <- seq(min(surface_data$life_exp), max(surface_data$life_exp), length.out = 30)
ys <- seq(min(surface_data$footprint), max(surface_data$footprint), length.out = 30)
grid <- expand.grid(life_exp = xs, footprint = ys)
z <- matrix(predict(surface_model, newdata = grid), nrow = length(xs))
persp(xs, ys, z, theta = 35, phi = 25, expand = 0.5,
      col = "lightblue", shade = 0.3, ticktype = "detailed",
      xlab = "Life expectancy", ylab = "Footprint", zlab = "Fitted HPI",
      cex.axis = 0.65, cex.lab = 0.8)







Figure 7: persp() projects a grid of fitted HPI values into a three-dimensional surface with a chosen viewing angle; this illustrative linear-model surface is not raw country data or the HPI formula, and some grid combinations may lack observations.





Life expectancy is measured in years and ecological footprint in global hectares per person. The fitted surface is a descriptive graphics demonstration, not a causal model.



2.3 Adding to an existing plot

points()

scatter <- hpi[complete.cases(hpi[c("gdp", "life_sat")]) &
                 hpi$continent %in% c("East Asia", "Western Europe"), ]
scatter$gdp_thousands <- scatter$gdp / 1000
regions <- c("East Asia", "Western Europe")
region_colors <- c("#0072B2", "#D55E00")
region_symbols <- c(16, 17)
group_id <- match(scatter$continent, regions)

# Reuse the same background and points in the following examples.
draw_scatter <- function() {
  plot(scatter$gdp_thousands, scatter$life_sat, type = "n",
       xlab = "GDP per capita (thousands, PPP international dollars), 2024",
       ylab = "Life satisfaction (0-10), 2024", ylim = c(3, 9))
  points(scatter$gdp_thousands, scatter$life_sat,
         col = region_colors[group_id], pch = region_symbols[group_id])
}
draw_scatter()







Figure 8: points() adds country observations to an existing coordinate system, using blue circles for East Asia and orange triangles for Western Europe.







lines()

trend <- lowess(scatter$gdp_thousands, scatter$life_sat)
draw_scatter()
lines(trend, col = "grey30", lwd = 2)







Figure 9: lines() connects ordered coordinates on an existing plot, here adding a LOWESS trend for the two displayed regions pooled together.








2.4 Annotating

text()

label_rows <- unique(c(which.min(scatter$life_sat), which.max(scatter$life_sat)))
add_country_labels <- function() {
  text(scatter$gdp_thousands[label_rows], scatter$life_sat[label_rows],
       labels = scatter$country[label_rows], pos = c(1, 3), cex = 0.8)
}
draw_scatter()
lines(trend, col = "grey30", lwd = 2)
add_country_labels()







Figure 10: text() places country labels at data coordinates inside the existing plot, here identifying the highest and lowest life satisfaction among the displayed countries.







mtext()

op <- par(mar = c(6, 4.5, 2, 1))
draw_scatter()
lines(trend, col = "grey30", lwd = 2)
add_country_labels()
mtext("Source: Happy Planet Index 2026; observations from 2024",
      side = 1, line = 4.5, cex = 0.8)
par(op)







Figure 11: mtext() adds a source note in the plot margin using a side and line offset, whereas text() positions labels using data coordinates.







legend()

op <- par(mar = c(6, 4.5, 2, 1))
draw_scatter()
lines(trend, col = "grey30", lwd = 2)
add_country_labels()
mtext("Source: Happy Planet Index 2026; observations from 2024",
      side = 1, line = 4.5, cex = 0.8)
legend("topright", legend = c(regions, "Pooled LOWESS trend"),
       col = c(region_colors, "grey30"), pch = c(region_symbols, NA),
       lty = c(NA, NA, 1), lwd = c(NA, NA, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(op)







Figure 12: legend() explains the colors, point symbols, and fitted line used in the existing plot.








A note on names()
names() is not a plotting function: it reads or sets an object’s names attribute, which functions such as pie() and barplot() can use as labels. It belongs to data preparation rather than drawing on a graphics device.

AI Use Statement
I used two AI tools for this assignment. Claude (Anthropic), in the Claude desktop app, helped me plan the assignment, build the line-by-line note template for Murrell’s chapter 1 code, check my answers to the questions in those notes, extract the 2024 subset of the Happy Planet Index workbook into hpi2024.csv (including the mapping from the workbook’s numeric continent codes to region names), and scaffold the structure of this page. Codex (OpenAI) turned my notes into an English draft, corrected misunderstandings about base graphics, and wrote the R plotting examples and figure captions from that scaffold. The observations in Section 1 come from my own line-by-line runs of the code; the wording, the plotting code, and the illustrative fitted surface were developed with AI assistance. I used AI to clarify the graphics concepts, to express my observations in English, and to keep the examples reproducible.
The full log of my exchange with Claude for this assignment is available here: Assignment 2: AI Use Log.

title: Assignment 2: AI Use Log
text:
Conversation Log — Claude

1. Understanding what Assignment 2 asks for

Me: 我覺得差不多要準備做 Assignment 2，考試準備到一個段落了。
(I think it is about time to start Assignment 2; my exam preparation has reached a stopping point.)

Claude: Read the handout and broke it into four tasks: run Murrell’s chapter 1 code line by line, exercise twelve plotting functions on my own data with one figure and one sentence each, use the Happy Planet Index filtered to a single year, and post the figures with the code that produced them. Estimated four to six hours and suggested splitting it over two days.


2. Getting the chapter 1 code

Me: (Shared the chapter 1 figure gallery page and reported that murrell01.R was not on Teams.)

Claude: The gallery links to separate .R files rather than one script, and Claude’s own network could not reach the site. It wrote an R script that reads the chapter page from my machine, extracts every .R link, downloads them, and concatenates them into a single murrell01.R. The first attempt found nothing because the page uses uppercase HREF; after Claude made the pattern case-insensitive, all 14 files downloaded (1,295 lines).

Me: (Reported system error 32 when opening the file.)

Claude: Diagnosed it as a file connection left open by the failed first run (close(con) never executed), and pointed out that this is the same discipline as png() needing dev.off(). closeAllConnections() or restarting R fixed it.


3. The note template

Me: 可以幫我生一個檔案有這樣的格式嗎？我這樣子邊執行邊看。可以幫我加上一些中文讓我理解的快速一些嗎？
(Can you generate a file in this format so I can fill it in while running the code? Can you add some Chinese so I understand faster?)

Claude: Built murrell01-notes.md, listing every line of the first two sections with a Chinese hint for each argument (mar, pch, bty, theta, phi), a column for what I observed on the device, and a type column (high-level / low-level / setting / data). Added six questions drawn from the code itself.






Note4. Checking my answers (most relevant)




Me: (Submitted my answers to the six questions.)

Claude: Confirmed two answers and corrected three:

text() before plot(): in a fresh session this is an error (plot.new has not been called yet); I had seen “the text does not appear” only because an old plot was still on the device.
What plot() does: it is plot.new() + plot.window() + drawing the data + axis(1) + axis(2) + box() + title(); my answer covered only the first step.
freq = FALSE: I had the direction backwards. On a count scale the density curve is compressed against the axis, because counts reach the teens while the density peaks near 0.4.
boxplot(add = TRUE): I said it still counted as high-level because it clears the plot. It does not clear the plot; with add = TRUE it behaves as a low-level call, which is why the two sets of boxes sit side by side.
midpts: my value was right; Claude added the reason it is needed — the bars are not at 1, 2, 3, 4, so the labels need the returned positions.
theta / phi: rotation versus viewing elevation.

Claude also filled in the type column for all 38 rows as a check against my own reading.








Note5. The data and the page scaffold (most relevant)




Me: 好的就 2024 年吧。
(All right, let’s use 2024.)

Claude: Checked how complete each year is and recommended 2024, because the GDP column is empty for 2025. Extracted the 2024 rows from the All Data sheet into hpi2024.csv (153 countries), and translated the workbook’s numeric continent codes into region names after verifying the order against the workbook’s own Cont data sheet. Reported the missing values I cite on the assignment page: life satisfaction 12, HPI 16, GDP 6, footprint 4. It also wrote 02_export_csv.R so the same extract is reproducible from the original workbook, and created the skeleton of assignment2.qmd with the twelve chunks and hints — including the suggestion to fit a smoothed surface for persp(), since that function needs a grid rather than country rows.




6. Reviewing the draft

Me: 是這樣嗎？幫我看一下。
(Is this right? Please take a look.)

Claude: Checked the page and the rendered output. Confirmed the code was correct, including the hpi ~ continent formula (the data frame and the column share a name) and the orientation of the persp() matrix. Asked for three changes, which I made: naming both AI tools in the statement rather than only Codex, adding Assignment 2 to the site navigation, and hiding the str() output in favour of a short preview table. It also added fig-alt text to all twelve figures for screen readers and sharpened the par() caption to say that the call draws nothing by itself.


7. Splitting the logs

Me: 我覺得要分開會比較好，ai-log 是 Assignment 1 的，另一個是 Assignment 2。
(I think it is better to separate them: ai-log for Assignment 1 and another one for Assignment 2.)

Claude: Created this page and linked it from the Assignment 2 page.

How and Why I Used AI

How: step-by-step guidance for setting up RStudio projects, running Fall.R and anscombe01.R, exporting figures, and adding a page to my Quarto website. I also used it to polish and translate my English writing, suggest regression diagnostics, and calculate percentage declines for the chart critique.

title: Assignment 1: AI Use Log
text:
Conversation Log

1. Catching up on readings and understanding the assignment

Me: 我目前閱讀只完成到 Week 2… 能否告訴我要下載哪些資料來閱讀呢？這個 assignment 要我做什麼呢？我已經把 R 還有網站環境處理好，也推上 GitHub 了，這是 assignment 要求的嗎？
(I have only finished the Week 2 readings. Which materials should I download? What does this assignment ask me to do? I have already set up R and my website and pushed to GitHub. Is that what the assignment requires?)

Claude: Listed the Week 3 readings (Cairo, The Truthful Art and How Charts Lie; Quarto closeread) and Week 4 readings (Ware ch. 1–3; Cleveland & McGill 1984; Heer & Bostock 2010), plus Anscombe (1973) for the assignment. Summarized the three assignment tasks. Explained that setting up the website is a prerequisite rather than the assignment itself, and reminded me to confirm that GitHub Pages is live and to include an AI appendix.


2. Disk space and folder organization

Me: 我的網站在 C 槽，但 C 槽快要滿了。R 的東西都在外接硬碟 F 槽，要怎麼處理比較好？
(My website is on drive C, which is almost full. My R files are on external drive F. What is the best way to handle this?)

Claude: Checked both folders. The website is only 3.5 MB, so it is not what fills drive C. Suggested keeping textbooks, scripts, and raw work on drive F and putting only final outputs (images, .qmd pages) in the website.


3. Deciding not to move the website

Me: 我傾向不搬，因為我已經繳交作業了，怕網址會亂掉。上傳東西會不會把槽弄滿？
(I prefer not to move it because I already submitted my website and worry the URL will break. Will uploading assignments fill the drive?)

Claude: Confirmed that the URL depends on the GitHub repository, not the local folder. Each assignment adds only a few hundred KB. Proposed the workflow: work on drive F, copy only final images to the website.


4. Running Fall.R and choosing winter colors

Me: (Shared console output and a screenshot of the default Fall plot.) 要存成圖片放到哪裡嗎？
(Where should I save the image?)

Claude: Suggested using ggsave() instead of right-click saving, and proposed a winter palette: lightsteelblue1 branches on a midnightblue background.


5. Creating a separate RStudio project on drive F

Me: 還是說要分開來用？我要重新打開 F 槽中的資料夾來執行，可否一步一步帶著我做？
(Should I use them separately? I want to open the folder on drive F as a project. Can you guide me step by step?)

Claude: Guided me to create an RStudio project in the course folder on drive F (File → New Project → Existing Directory), so relative paths save outputs there.


6. Understanding the code changes

Me: 為什麼要改這些東西呢？
(Why do these things need to be changed?)

Claude: Explained each change: branch color (task 2a), background color for contrast, storing the plot in p, and ggsave() to export the file (task 2b). Suggested other winter color combinations.


7. Running an entire script

Me: R 不能一次執行全部嗎？
(Can’t R run the whole script at once?)

Claude: Explained Ctrl+Shift+Enter (Source with Echo), Ctrl+A then Ctrl+Enter, and the Source button.


8. Exporting the Anscombe figure

Me: (Shared winter.png, then the full console output of anscombe01.R.) 另外我想知道你改的那些是什麼意思。
(I also want to know what your changes mean.)

Claude: Confirmed both images were saved. Explained png() and dev.off() for base R graphics, and the par(mfrow = c(2, 2)) layout. Summarized the regression output: all four data sets have mean x = 9, mean y = 7.5, and fitted line y = 3 + 0.5x with R² = 0.67.


9. Why the Plots pane showed four separate plots

Me: 為什麼 plot 裡面並不是出現一張圖而是四張圖呢？
(Why does the Plots pane show four plots instead of one?)

Claude: Explained that the “simple version” draws four separate plots in RStudio, while the 2×2 panel is written directly to the PNG file.


10. Adding the Assignment 1 page to the website

Me: 我有這兩張圖，接下來要如何進行呢？
(I have both images. What should I do next?)

Claude: Guided me to copy the images into images/, create assignment1.qmd, add it to the navbar in _quarto.yml, and dismiss the RStudio “save workspace” prompt. Recommended setting RStudio to never save .RData.


11. Rendering the whole website

Me: 我是使用這個按鈕，點完之後跳出網頁。
(I used this Render button, and a web page opened.)

title: EPPS 6356 Assignment 1
text:
Anscombe’s four regression data sets


Anscombe’s quartet (Anscombe 1973) shows that summary statistics can oversimplify data. The four data sets share nearly identical statistical properties: the mean of x is 9, the mean of y is 7.5, the correlation is 0.816, and every fitted regression line is y = 3 + 0.5x with an R² of 0.67. Because these numbers are only summaries, they suggest the four data sets are the same. The scatter plots, however, reveal four different structures: data set 1 is roughly linear, data set 2 is clearly curved, data set 3 is a near-perfect line distorted by one outlier, and in data set 4 a single extreme point creates the entire slope. A linear regression is only appropriate for the first case. Anscombe’s own solution is to make both calculations and graphs: scatterplot the data before any regression, plot the residuals against the fitted values after fitting, transform the variables or add a quadratic term when the relation is curved (data set 2), check whether outliers are recording errors (data set 3), and when one observation strongly influences the result, report the regression both with and without it (data set 4).

text:
3. Chart Critique



Market Capitalization of the World’s Biggest Banks. Source: Cairo (2012), Figure 2.8.


This chart uses nested bubbles to compare the market value of 15 banks in January 2007 and January 2009. The problem is that people judge length much more accurately than area. For example, Société Générale’s value fell from $80 billion to $26 billion, but it is hard to tell from the bubbles that the inner circle is only about one-third of the outer one. As Cairo shows, a bar chart makes this comparison much easier. Bubble charts are popular and look attractive, but designers often choose them by following trends rather than asking what the reader needs to see.
I would go one step further. The real story in this data is how much each bank lost, yet neither the bubble chart nor a simple bar chart shows the percentage decline directly. RBS lost 96% of its value, Citigroup 93%, and Barclays 92%, while Santander lost only 45%. These differences are almost invisible in the bubbles. A bar chart of percentage change, sorted from largest to smallest loss, or a dumbbell chart connecting the 2007 and 2009 values, would let readers see immediately which banks were hit hardest by the financial crisis.

Research Project

Weather Forecasting with Fourier Neural Operators
This project investigates the use of Fourier Neural Operators and related deep-learning architectures for spatiotemporal weather forecasting.
Data-generating process. The data are derived from ERA5, a global atmospheric reanalysis dataset produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). ERA5 combines historical observations from satellites, weather stations, and other instruments with numerical weather prediction models to generate consistent estimates of atmospheric conditions over time.
